question.prompt: Triangle \(ABC\) has \(\angle BAC = 60^\circ,\) \(\angle CBA \le 90^\circ,\) \(BC = 1,\) and \(AC \ge AB.\) Let \(H,\) \(I,\) and \(O\) be the orthocenter, incenter, and circumcenter of \(\triangle ABC,\) respectively. Assume that the area of the pentagon \(BCOIH\) is the maximum possible. What is \(\angle CBA?\)

solutions.explanation:
The useful observation is that the three centers see the fixed segment \(BC\) under the same angle. This places them on one fixed circle and turns the area problem into a simpler problem about points moving along an arc.

Write \(\beta=\angle CBA\) and \(\gamma=\angle BCA\). Since \(AC\ge AB\), their opposite angles satisfy \(\beta\ge\gamma\). Together with \(\beta+\gamma=120^\circ\) and \(\beta\le90^\circ\), this gives
\[
60^\circ\le\beta\le90^\circ,\qquad \gamma=120^\circ-\beta.
\]
Fix \(BC\), taking \(A\) above it; reflection does not change any area. The circumcenter satisfies \(OB=OC\) and \(\angle BOC=120^\circ\), by the inscribed-angle theorem. Hence the base angles of \(\triangle BOC\) are \(30^\circ\). Thus \(O\) is fixed as \(A\) varies.

The angle-bisector property of the incenter gives
\[
\angle BIC=180^\circ-\frac{\beta+\gamma}{2}=120^\circ.
\]
For \(\beta<90^\circ\), the triangle is acute. Its altitudes through \(B\) and \(C\) give
\[
\angle BHC=180^\circ-\angle BAC=120^\circ.
\]
The points \(O,I,H\) are above \(BC\). By the converse of the inscribed-angle theorem, they lie on the same circular arc through \(B\) and \(C\). Call this fixed circle \(\Gamma\).

We can also locate their order along the arc. The relevant angles at \(B\) are
\[
\angle CBO=30^\circ,\qquad
\angle CBI=\frac\beta2,\qquad
\angle CBH=90^\circ-\gamma=\beta-30^\circ.
\]
Thus their order is \(C,O,I,H,B\), allowing coincidences at an endpoint. Since \(\angle OCB=30^\circ\), the minor arc \(OB\) of \(\Gamma\) measures \(60^\circ\). Put \(t=\beta-60^\circ\). Applying the inscribed-angle theorem to the differences of the displayed angles gives the successive arc measures
\[
\widehat{OI}=t,\qquad \widehat{IH}=t,\qquad \widehat{HB}=60^\circ-2t.
\]
Here \(0^\circ\le t\le30^\circ\). At \(\beta=60^\circ\), the triangle is equilateral and \(O=I=H\). At \(\beta=90^\circ\), \(H=B\), and the arc gaps are directly \(30^\circ,30^\circ,0^\circ\). We may include these collapsed polygons when making an upper-bound comparison.

The pentagon's area is the fixed area of \(\triangle BCO\) plus the area of \(OIHB\). Enlarge the comparison family by allowing two arbitrary ordered points \(X,Y\) on the minor arc \(OB\), and maximize the area of \(OXYB\). A maximum exists because the points range over a closed arc and area varies continuously. Coincident vertices cannot maximize the area: inserting a vertex into a nonzero arc adds a positive triangular area.

With \(O,Y,B\) fixed, moving \(X\) changes only the area of \(\triangle OXY\). Its base \(OY\) is fixed, so its area is greatest when its height is greatest. On the minor arc \(OY\), the point farthest from chord \(OY\) is the arc midpoint, on the chord's perpendicular bisector. Therefore a maximizing \(X\) must bisect arc \(OY\). Applying the same argument to \(Y\), with \(O,X,B\) fixed, shows that \(Y\) must bisect arc \(XB\).

These two midpoint conditions force
\[
\widehat{OX}=\widehat{XY}=\widehat{YB}=20^\circ.
\]
This best configuration belongs to the original family: take \(t=20^\circ\), so \(\beta=80^\circ\) and \(\gamma=40^\circ\). A triangle with angles \(60^\circ,80^\circ,40^\circ\) and \(BC=1\) exists, satisfies every stated condition, and has exactly these three arc gaps. Therefore the maximum occurs at \(\boxed{80^\circ}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Place the centers on one circle and equalize the arc gaps
Locate the centers, compute area, and factor its difference from the maximum
